issues.legal_issue: Publication of substituted summons in a widely circulated local newspaper other than the newspaper specified by the court does not invalidate service merely because of that deviation.
material_facts: The trial court ordered substituted service by publication in a local daily.
The summons was instead published in another local daily, and the evidence showed that both newspapers were widely circulated in the area.
issues.conclusion: The change of newspaper was a mere irregularity and did not invalidate the substituted service or justify setting aside the ex-parte decree on that ground alone.
issues.legal_principle: Under the second proviso to Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an ex-parte decree cannot be set aside merely because of an irregularity in service. Where the newspaper used for substituted service is widely circulated in the area, using it instead of the newspaper specified by the court does not materially affect service. The court’s satisfaction for ordering substituted service may be implicit in its order. No earlier cases were relied on for this ruling.

predicates.ex_parte_decree_set_aside_proceeding: A party sought to set aside a decree entered when that party did not appear.
predicates.substituted_summons_published_in_another: The summons was published in a local newspaper different from the one specified by the court.
predicates.both_papers_widely_circulated: The newspaper specified by the court and the newspaper actually used were both widely circulated in the relevant area.

issues.definition: When a party seeks to set aside a decree entered in its absence and substituted summons was published in a different but equally widely circulated local paper, the newspaper deviation does not invalidate service.

issues.legal_issue: Properly addressed, prepaid summons sent by registered post with acknowledgement due may be presumed served when the acknowledgement is not received, unless the recipient rebuts that presumption with convincing evidence.
material_facts: The summonses were sent by registered post with acknowledgement due to the defendants’ correct addresses, and it was not disputed that they were properly addressed, prepaid, and duly sent.
One defendant gave only a bare statement that he had not received the registered letter and did not call the postman, while the other defendant gave no evidence to rebut service.
The defendants occupied the premises jointly, and the circumstances made it inherently improbable that the registered summons would have been served on one but not the other.
issues.conclusion: The presumption of service was not rebutted; the registered summonses were treated as duly served, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The second proviso to Order 5 Rule 19A of the Code of Civil Procedure and Section 27 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 provide for a presumption of due service when summons is properly addressed, prepaid, and duly sent by registered post with acknowledgement due, even if the acknowledgement is not received within the specified period. The presumption is rebuttable, and the recipient must produce convincing and cogent evidence to rebut it. Under Order 9 Rule 13, an applicant must establish both that summons was not duly served and that sufficient cause prevented appearance; the latter condition was not at issue here. No earlier cases were relied on.

rule.if: ex_parte_decree_set_aside_proceeding and registered_summons_correctly_addressed and registered_summons_prepaid_and_duly_sent and acknowledgment_not_received and service_presumption_not_rebutted

predicates.ex_parte_decree_set_aside_proceeding: A party sought to set aside a decree entered when that party did not appear.
predicates.registered_summons_correctly_addressed: The summons sent by registered post was addressed to the recipient’s correct address.
predicates.registered_summons_prepaid_and_duly_sent: The registered summons was prepaid and duly sent with acknowledgement due.
predicates.acknowledgment_not_received: The court did not receive the acknowledgement of delivery within the applicable period.
predicates.service_presumption_not_rebutted: The recipient did not provide convincing and cogent evidence showing that the registered summons was not served.

issues.definition: In a proceeding to set aside a decree entered in a party’s absence, a correctly addressed, prepaid, duly sent registered summons is treated as served when its acknowledgement is not received and the recipient does not convincingly rebut service.
